title: IP Authentication Header
summary: Describes an updated version of the IP Authentication Header, which provides authentication services in IPv4 and IPv6. It replaces RFC 2402 and is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: The IP Authentication Header (AH) lets IPsec endpoints check that a packet came from a peer with the right security association and was not changed. It can also reject replayed packets, but it does not encrypt their contents.

questions: what is the ipsec authentication header
ah transport mode vs tunnel mode
subtitle: Add integrity checks and optional replay protection to IP packets.

tldr.problem: IP packets need a way to verify their origin and detect changes, including changes to IP-header fields that remain predictable in transit.
tldr.mechanism: The Authentication Header carries a Security Parameters Index, sequence number, and Integrity Check Value; endpoints compute and verify the value using their Security Association.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4302 obsoletes RFC 2402. AH provides integrity and data-origin authentication, with optional anti-replay checks, but does not encrypt packets.

today: RFC 4302 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2402. It specifies the IP Authentication Header for IPv4 and IPv6.

sections.title: What AH Protects
sections.content:
The IP Authentication Header (AH) provides connectionless integrity and data-origin authentication for IPv4 and IPv6 datagrams. A receiver may also enable protection against replayed packets for a Security Association (SA).

AH authenticates as much of the IP header as possible and the next-level data. Fields that can change unpredictably while a packet travels cannot be protected, so header protection is partial.
sections.plainLanguage: AH helps a receiver detect packet changes and verify the packet's source. It cannot protect fields that routers may change unpredictably.

sections.title: The Authentication Header Fields
sections.content:
The AH header contains Next Header, Payload Length, a reserved field, the Security Parameters Index (SPI), a Sequence Number, and a variable-length Integrity Check Value (ICV). The preceding IP header identifies AH with protocol or next-header value 51.

The SPI helps the receiver find the Security Association. The sequence number supports replay checks when the receiver enables them, and the ICV is computed over the protected packet fields with its own field zeroed during calculation.
sections.plainLanguage: The header identifies the security association, numbers the packet, and carries a check value. The receiver uses these fields to decide how to verify the packet.

sections.title: Transport Mode and Tunnel Mode
sections.content:
In transport mode, AH is placed after the IP header and before the next protocol, such as TCP or UDP. In tunnel mode, an outer IP header carries the security peers' addresses, while AH protects the inner IP packet.

In either mode, AH processing uses the Security Association selected for the packet. IPv4 fragments are reassembled before AH verification; packets that still appear fragmented when offered to AH are discarded.
sections.plainLanguage: Transport mode adds AH to one IP packet. Tunnel mode protects an inner packet carried inside a new outer IP packet.

sections.title: Calculating and Checking the ICV
sections.content:
The sender calculates an ICV over immutable or predictable IP fields, the AH header, and the packet data. Fields that may change in transit are set to zero for the calculation; the receiver applies the same rules and compares the result with the received ICV.

If the values do not match, the receiver discards the datagram. With Extended Sequence Numbers, the high-order 32 bits are included in the calculation but are not sent in the AH header.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender and receiver calculate the same check value from the protected parts of the packet. If the values differ, the receiver rejects the packet.

sections.title: Rejecting Replayed Packets
sections.content:
Anti-replay is available for each Security Association and is enabled or disabled by the receiver. When enabled, the receiver tracks sequence numbers in a sliding window and rejects duplicates or numbers that fall too far behind.

The sender must not let an enabled sequence number wrap. An Extended Sequence Number option uses a 64-bit count but sends only the low-order 32 bits in each packet; the high-order part is maintained by the endpoints.
sections.plainLanguage: A receiver can remember recently accepted packet numbers and reject a repeated packet. Extended sequence numbers let that count continue past the 32-bit value sent in the header.
